text.en: FADE IN:

A wide meadow under a high sun. A HARE lounges in tall grass, watching a TORTOISE make slow, deliberate progress across the field. A FOX and a HEDGEHOG look on from a fallen log, and a small cluster of SPARROWS observes from a nearby branch, unbothered by any of it.
(laughing)
At that pace you'll arrive at next spring's flowers, not this one's.
(not stopping, not even glancing over)
I'll arrive, all the same. That's rather the whole point of walking.
Arriving isn't much of an achievement if it takes a season to manage.
(from the log, amused)
He has a point, Tortoise. You are remarkably unhurried, even for a tortoise.
Unhurried isn't the same as unable.
Care to prove it, then? A race - that oak at the field's edge to the old fence post by the stream.
(finally stopping, considering him)
If you like.
(sitting up, delighted)
Oh, this I have to see.
The Fox hops down from the log, tail flicking with anticipation.
I'll call the start, if no one minds a fair fox for it. I've refereed worse arrangements.
Someone ought to referee this one properly. He'll never let it go otherwise.
(stretching, entirely unbothered)
There's nothing to let go of. I haven't lost a race since I learned to run.
Then this will be a fine place to start keeping count.

Word has travelled fast. A modest crowd of field creatures has gathered at the oak - the Sparrows overhead, a family of RABBITS peering from a hedge, an old OWL blinking sleepily from a low branch. Hare and Tortoise line up at the oak's roots. Fox raises a paw between them.
On my word, and not a heartbeat before. Ready -
(already bouncing on his heels)
Born ready. Practically finished, if we're honest.
- go!
The Hare is gone in a blur of dust and flattened grass. The Tortoise sets off at exactly the pace he started at, neither faster nor slower for the crowd watching.
(to no one in particular)
This won't take long to decide, one way or the other.
(overlapping, unconvinced)
It never does. / Every single time.
The Hare, now a considerable distance ahead, slows to a trot, then a walk, glancing back over one shoulder at the empty field behind him. No sign of the Tortoise at all.
(to himself, thoroughly pleased)
He hasn't even reached the stream yet, and here I am, halfway to finished and hardly out of breath.
He spots a patch of clover, wanders over, and samples a mouthful without any particular urgency.
A wide oak throws a deep, inviting shade a little off the race path. The Hare drops into the cool grass beneath it, more amused than tired, stretching out at full length.
(yawning)
A short rest changes nothing. I could sleep till supper and still cross that fence post walking.
He closes his eyes. Somewhere in the distance, unhurried and entirely unaware of being underestimated, small clawed feet continue their steady progress across the field.

The light has shifted, long shadows now stretching where there were none before. The Hare sleeps on, one ear twitching at some distant birdsong. In the middle distance, small and steady, the Tortoise passes beneath the very same oak without so much as a glance in his direction.
(quietly, mostly to himself, not stopping)
Sleep well.
He continues on, unhurried, toward the fence post now visible at the field's far edge.

The crowd has drifted down the field to get a better view of the finish - Fox pacing, Hedgehog perched on a stone, the Rabbits whispering among themselves, the Owl now fully awake and visibly invested.
(squinting)
Is that - I think that's the Tortoise. Alone.
(craning his neck)
Where in the world is the Hare?
(overlapping again)
Maybe he's already finished. / He'd have said something, surely.
The Tortoise plods steadily into view, entirely unhurried, exactly as he's looked the whole race.
The fence post stands weathered and grey at the field's far edge. The Tortoise reaches it and, without any ceremony at all, touches it with one foot.
(quietly, to no one)
There, then.

The gathered crowd erupts - the Rabbits thumping their feet, the Sparrows scattering upward in a startled cloud, the Owl hooting once in what might be approval. Fox and Hedgehog arrive a moment later, both a little out of breath from hurrying down the field.
Where's the Hare?
(pointing back the way they came)
Asleep under the big oak, unless I miss my guess entirely.
The Hare comes tearing across the field a moment later, ears flat with alarm, and skids to a stop at the sight of the Tortoise already resting comfortably against the post.
That's - how did you - I only closed my eyes for a moment!
(settling in for a rest of his own, unbothered)
A moment was all it took, it seems.
(deflated, sitting heavily in the grass)
I don't understand it. I'm faster in every single way that matters.
Every way but the one that decided the race.
(not unkindly)
Fast is a fine thing to be, Hare. But it isn't the same thing as finished.
The crowd has mostly wandered off, the excitement settling into ordinary afternoon again. The Hare sits beside the Tortoise now, chastened, watching the sun sink toward the tree line.
Same race, next spring? I'd like the chance to do it properly this time.
(a small, patient smile)
Anytime you like. I'll be walking the same pace either way.
Slow and steady. It adds up, doesn't it.
It generally does, in the end.
FADE OUT.
